article.title: GitHub Cuts Public Bug Bounty Payouts in Half, Steering Top Rewards to a New Invite-Only VIP Tier
article.summary: GitHub is halving public bug bounty payouts and moving its highest rewards behind an invite-only VIP tier, citing a flood of low-effort and AI-generated reports.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

GitHub is overhauling its bug bounty program, cutting public payouts roughly in half at every severity level while opening a new invite-only tier that pays established researchers significantly more, according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). The changes take effect July 27, 2026, and follow an earlier round of restrictions the company introduced in May. GitHub says the goal is to reduce the volume of low-effort and AI-generated submissions clogging its review queue, as reported by [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html).

## What We Know

Under the restructuring, GitHub's public program will pay a fixed $250 for low-severity findings, $2,000 for medium, $5,000 for high, and $10,000 for critical vulnerabilities, according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). That replaces variable ranges that previously ran as high as $2,000 for low-severity reports, $4,000 to $10,000 for medium, $10,000 to $20,000 for high, and $20,000 to $30,000-plus for critical findings, per [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html). The outlet calculated that the new public rates come out to roughly 50 percent lower for medium, high, and critical findings and about 59 percent lower for low-severity reports, measured against the bottom of GitHub's previous ranges.

Researchers who qualify can instead be invited into a new permanent VIP tier, which pays $1,000 for low-severity findings, $7,500 for medium, $20,000 for high, and $30,000 or more for critical vulnerabilities — matching or exceeding the top of the old public ranges, according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). To qualify, a researcher needs at least one critical finding, two high-severity findings, four medium findings, or seven low-severity findings, though [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html) notes meeting the threshold does not guarantee an invitation. GitHub framed the philosophy behind the split bluntly: "You don't earn more by submitting more. You earn more by submitting better," the company wrote in [its announcement](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/).

GitHub is also adding what it calls "a HackerOne signal requirement on the public program" specifically "to reduce the volume of low-effort and AI-generated reports," according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). Reports submitted before July 27 will still be paid under the old terms, [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html) reported.

The July changes build on a policy update GitHub made in May. In a post titled "Raising the bar," Senior Product Security Engineer Jarom Brown announced that submissions would need "a working proof of concept with demonstrated security impact," and that low-impact reports resulting only in code or documentation improvements would earn "GitHub swag rather than a bounty payout," according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/raising-the-bar-quality-shared-responsibility-and-the-future-of-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). Brown said GitHub has no objection to researchers using AI tools, writing "we have no problem with researchers using AI tools," and that "an AI-assisted finding that's been verified, reproduced, and submitted with a working proof of concept is a great submission." [CSO Online](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4173224/github-scales-back-bug-bounty-reminds-users-security-is-their-responsibility-too.html) independently confirmed Brown's quotes and reported that the May changes followed a sharp rise, over the prior year, in submissions lacking meaningful security impact — a trend GitHub attributed largely to generative AI tools. Brown told CSO Online that "not every valid submission represents a meaningful security risk."

GitHub is not alone in confronting this problem. [CSO Online](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4173224/github-scales-back-bug-bounty-reminds-users-security-is-their-responsibility-too.html) reported that Curl, HackerOne, and Google have each implemented their own restrictions on AI-assisted submissions amid rising volume. [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html) reported that Curl maintainer Daniel Stenberg ended the project's cash bug bounty at the end of January 2026 after its confirmed-vulnerability rate fell below 5 percent amid a rise in AI-generated junk reports — a shutdown [previously reported](/article/2026-02/22-ai-generated-slop-is-overwhelming-open-source-projects-forcing-emergency-countermeasures) by The Machine Herald. Since curl removed the cash incentive, the outlet reported, reports have been arriving at about twice the 2025 rate, with 15 to 16 percent confirmed as vulnerabilities; Stenberg said almost every report now appears AI-assisted and most are high quality.

## What We Don't Know

GitHub has not disclosed how many researchers currently qualify for the new VIP tier or how many total submissions its public program receives that it considers low-effort or AI-generated. [CSO Online](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4173224/github-scales-back-bug-bounty-reminds-users-security-is-their-responsibility-too.html) reported that some industry analysts have warned the shift away from cash rewards for lower-severity findings could discourage participation from newer, independent researchers who rely on smaller bounty payments, though the practical effect on submission volume and quality after the July 27 changes take hold remains to be seen.

## Analysis

The restructuring illustrates how the same AI-driven submission flood that forced cURL to abandon cash bounties altogether is now reshaping incentives at one of the industry's largest bug bounty operators. Rather than eliminating cash rewards, GitHub is trying a more targeted fix: shrinking the public program's payouts while carving out a smaller, invite-only pool of proven researchers who can still earn the largest rewards. Whether a HackerOne signal requirement is enough to filter out AI-generated noise without discouraging legitimate newcomers from ever reaching VIP status is the open question the July 27 rollout will start to answer.
